passages.t: Four beasts from the sea, and a little horn
passages.happening:
In the first year of Belshazzar's reign, Daniel has a dream and visions as he lies in bed, and he writes them down (verse 1).

He sees the four winds of heaven churning up the great sea, and four great beasts coming up out of it, each different from the others (verses 2-3). The first is like a lion with eagle's wings. Its wings are torn off, and it is made to stand on two feet like a man and given a man's mind (verse 4). The second is like a bear, raised on one side, with three ribs in its mouth (verse 5). The third is like a leopard with four wings and four heads, and it is given authority to rule (verse 6).

Then a fourth beast appears, ‘dreadful and extremely strong’ with ‘large iron teeth’ (verse 7). It devours and crushes and tramples whatever is left. It is different from all the others, and it has ten horns.

While Daniel is looking at the horns, a little horn comes up among them, and three of the first horns are uprooted. ‘This horn had eyes like those of a man and a mouth that spoke words of arrogance’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
This chapter is the hinge of the book. It is the last chapter in Aramaic, so it completes the unit that began in chapter 2, and it retells the four-part statue as four beasts. It is also the first of Daniel's own visions. It steps back in time to Belshazzar's first year, probably about 553 BC, before the fall of Babylon in chapter 5.

The sea churned by the winds draws on a picture shared across the ancient world: the sea as the realm of chaos and hostile power. The Old Testament speaks of God's victory over the sea and its monsters. Beasts made of different animals were familiar from Babylonian and Assyrian art. Great winged bulls and lions with human heads guarded Assyrian palace gates, and Babylon's Ishtar Gate was faced with glazed-brick lions and dragons. To a reader in Babylon, the vision took the empire's own symbols of power and turned them into monsters.

Horns were the standard picture of strength and royal power, so a beast with ten horns is a power with many kings. A horn with eyes and a mouth is a king who sees and speaks with arrogance.

Where chapter 2 showed the kingdoms as a statue a king admired, chapter 7 shows them as God sees them: predatory beasts. The first beast, made to stand like a man and given a man's mind, recalls Nebuchadnezzar's humbling in chapter 4.
passages.later: Revelation combines Daniel's four beasts into one: ‘a beast with ten horns and seven heads rising out of the sea’ that ‘was like a leopard, with the feet of a bear and the mouth of a lion’ (Revelation 13:1-2). The prophets had pictured Babylon's king as a lion and as a great eagle (Jeremiah 4:7; Ezekiel 17:3).
passages.hard:
Which kingdoms are the four beasts, and who is the little horn?

The chapter explains them only as four kings or kingdoms (verses 17 and 23). The first is taken by interpreters of every school as Babylon. The traditional Jewish and Christian reading takes the bear as Media-Persia, the leopard as Greece and the fourth beast as Rome. That reading is already present in 4 Ezra, in Josephus and in the Talmud. Most critical scholars read the bear as Media, the leopard as Persia and the fourth beast as the Greek empire of Alexander and his successors, with the ten horns as kings of the Seleucid line in Syria and the little horn as Antiochus IV (175 to 164 BC). Futurist interpreters add that the little horn, or a figure it foreshadows, is a final opponent of God still to come.

These notes take no side among these readings. And they name no person, nation or movement of the present day as the little horn or any of the beasts. The history of reading Daniel is full of confident identifications with emperors, popes, sultans and modern rulers, and every one of them has passed.
passages.asks: The empires look like gold in chapter 2 and like beasts in chapter 7. Ask which powers in your world you admire that God might see as beasts. And ask what it would mean to see them that way without fear.

passages.t: The Ancient of Days, and one like a son of man
passages.happening:
The scene turns to heaven. ‘As I continued to watch, thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days took His seat’ (verse 9). His clothing is white as snow and his hair like pure wool. His throne is flaming with fire, its wheels ablaze. A river of fire flows from his presence, and thousands upon thousands attend him. ‘The court was convened, and the books were opened’ (verse 10).

Daniel keeps watching because of the horn's arrogant words. The beast is slain and its body thrown into the fire (verse 11). The other beasts lose their dominion, though they live on for a time (verse 12).

Then: ‘In my vision in the night I continued to watch, and I saw One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven. He approached the Ancient of Days and was led into His presence’ (verse 13). ‘And He was given dominion, glory, and kingship, that the people of every nation and language should serve Him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion that will not pass away, and His kingdom is one that will never be destroyed’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The heavenly scenes are written as poetry, in balanced lines, while the beasts are described in prose. The heavenly court uses royal and legal pictures Israel knew: God enthroned among his council, the judge taking his seat, the books opened by which the court decides. The Ancient of Days, aged, with white clothing and hair, speaks of dignity and eternity. His fiery throne with wheels recalls Ezekiel's vision of God's chariot-throne.

The plural thrones puzzled later readers. The Talmud reports that Rabbi Akiva explained them as one for God and one for David, that is, the Messiah, and was rebuked for it.

The phrase son of man, bar enash in Aramaic, ordinarily means simply a human being. The phrase has no article here: it is one like a son of man, a comparison, not yet a title. What is remarkable is that this human figure comes with the clouds of heaven, which elsewhere in the Old Testament carry God himself, and that all peoples serve him with a verb Daniel otherwise uses for the worship of God.

The chapter's great contrast is between beastly rule, which devours and tramples, and human rule, which receives its kingdom from God. It reverses Genesis 1, where humanity is made to rule over the beasts. Here the beasts have seized rule, and God gives it back to one like a son of man.
passages.later: At his trial Jesus joined this verse to Psalm 110: ‘you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven’ (Mark 14:62). He spoke of the end in the same words: ‘they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and glory’ (Mark 13:26). And Stephen, as he died, said, ‘I see heaven open and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God’ (Acts 7:56).
passages.hard:
Who is the one like a son of man?

The strongest case against the Christian reading comes from the chapter itself. The interpreter never mentions the son of man again. Instead, the kingdom is given to ‘the saints of the Most High’ (verse 18) and to ‘the people, the saints of the Most High’ (verse 27). Since the beasts stand for kingdoms, many scholars conclude that the human figure stands for a people, faithful Israel, and many Jewish interpreters have read him that way. John Collins takes another route and identifies him with an angel, most likely Michael, Israel's heavenly prince.

The traditional Jewish and Christian reading answers that a king in the ancient world could stand for his people, just as the beasts are called both kings and kingdoms, so the son of man can be an individual whose kingdom his people share. It points to what sets him apart: he comes with the clouds, as only God does, and receives the service Daniel elsewhere gives only to God. That individual reading appears early in Jewish writing, in the Similitudes of Enoch and 4 Ezra, in the Talmud's Messiah who comes with the clouds, and in Rashi.

These readings are not wholly exclusive, and the New Testament holds several together: Jesus is the Son of Man who receives the kingdom, and his people share it. These notes set out each reading in its own terms.
passages.asks: The kingdom in this chapter is given, not seized. Ask what you are trying to seize that God means to give. And ask what it means for you that history ends not with a beast but with a human face.

passages.t: Daniel asks the meaning, and the horn wars against the saints
passages.happening:
‘I, Daniel, was grieved in my spirit, and the visions in my mind alarmed me’ (verse 15). He goes to one of those standing near and asks what it all means (verse 16).

The answer is brief. ‘These four great beasts are four kings who will arise from the earth’ (verse 17). ‘But the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom and possess it forever’ (verse 18).

Daniel wants to know more about the fourth beast, with its iron teeth and bronze claws, and about the ten horns and the other horn, the one with eyes and a boastful mouth, before which three fell (verses 19-20). As he watched, ‘this horn was waging war against the saints and prevailing against them’ (verse 21), ‘until the Ancient of Days arrived and pronounced judgment in favor of the saints of the Most High, and the time came for them to possess the kingdom’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
The interpretation comes in two rounds, a brief one and a longer one focused on the fourth beast and the little horn. The second round adds details not in the vision, the bronze claws and the horn's war against the saints, so that the explanation deepens the vision rather than simply decoding it.

The saints are the holy ones of the Most High. Most interpreters read them as God's faithful people on earth, since they are persecuted and defeated by the horn. Some, notably John Collins, argue that they are angels. Some take the phrase to include both, the heavenly host and the earthly people who share its cause.

Verse 21 is honest. The horn wages war against the saints and prevails, for a time. The first hearers were not promised that they would be spared persecution. They were promised a limit to it, a judge over it, and a kingdom beyond it.

Daniel himself is not comforted. He is grieved and alarmed. The book gives believers permission to be shaken by what they know.
passages.later: Revelation takes up the words of verse 21 for the church: the beast ‘was permitted to wage war against the saints and to conquer them’ (Revelation 13:7). And Daniel's last vision promises, ‘There will be a time of distress, the likes of which will not have occurred from the beginning of nations until that time’ (Daniel 12:1), and then deliverance.
passages.asks: Daniel was troubled by what he saw, and he asked. Ask what in Scripture troubles you, and whether you bring your questions to God or leave them alone. And ask whether you believe the promise of verse 22 when the horn seems to be winning.

passages.t: The fourth kingdom, a time, and times, and half a time
passages.happening:
The interpreter explains. ‘The fourth beast is a fourth kingdom that will appear on the earth, different from all the other kingdoms, and it will devour the whole earth, trample it down, and crush it’ (verse 23). The ten horns are ten kings from that kingdom. After them another king will rise, different from the others, and subdue three kings (verse 24).

‘He will speak out against the Most High and oppress the saints of the Most High, intending to change the appointed times and laws; and the saints will be given into his hand for a time, and times, and half a time’ (verse 25).

‘But the court will convene, and his dominion will be taken away and completely destroyed forever’ (verse 26). Then the kingdom and dominion of all the kingdoms under heaven ‘will be given to the people, the saints of the Most High’ (verse 27). God's kingdom will be everlasting, and all rulers will serve and obey him.

‘Thus ends the matter’ (verse 28). Daniel's thoughts trouble him greatly, his face turns pale, and he keeps the matter to himself.
passages.hearers:
A time, and times, and half a time is usually taken as three and a half years: half of seven, a limited and broken period. The phrase returns in 12:7, and Revelation gives the same span as forty-two months and 1,260 days. The persecution is real, but it has an end set by God.

The details of the king in verse 25 fit Antiochus IV closely, which is the main reason for the critical reading. In 167 BC he outlawed the Sabbath, the festivals, circumcision and the temple sacrifices, an attempt to change the appointed times and laws. The temple was rededicated about three years later, in 164 BC, and he died the same year. Those who hold the traditional date answer that the chapter's scope is larger than one king, and that its fourth kingdom fits Rome's reach and endurance better.

The chapter ends not with Daniel's understanding but with his distress. He goes pale and keeps it to himself. The vision is a comfort for the long run, but it does not make the present easy.
passages.later: Revelation uses the same span for the season of the church under pressure: the woman is protected ‘for a time, and times, and half a time’ (Revelation 12:14). The same span returns at the end of Daniel, when an angel swears that it will be ‘for a time, and times, and half a time’ (Daniel 12:7).
passages.hard:
Does a time, and times, and half a time give a date for the end?

No date can be calculated from it, and these notes calculate none. In apocalyptic writing numbers are first of all symbols. Three and a half, half of seven, speaks of a time of trouble that is real but cut short. Readers who take the king of verse 25 as Antiochus see the period fulfilled in the years between the desecration of 167 BC and the rededication of 164 BC. Readers who see the vision reaching further read it as the season of trouble before the end, however long that season runs. Readers of Revelation take it up as the life of the church under pressure.

The long history of attempts to date the end from these numbers is a warning. Jesus said that no one knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36), and every date set by calculation has passed. These notes name no person or power of the present day as the king of this chapter.
passages.asks: The persecution in this chapter is real and limited. Ask how believing that God sets a limit to suffering could change the way you face it. And ask whether you are more interested in calculating the end than in being faithful until it comes.
